name: Power-assisted liposuction (PAL)
lead: Power-assisted liposuction (PAL) is a variant of suction lipectomy in which the cannula is driven by a motor so that it vibrates or reciprocates rapidly while the surgeon moves it through subcutaneous fat. It is one of several liposuction techniques, alongside tumescent, ultrasound-assisted, laser-assisted and water-jet-assisted methods.[1]

Proponents of the technique say the mechanical motion lets surgeons remove fat with less manual effort, and it has been described in published surgical reports for body contouring, superficial liposuction, gynecomastia in men and fat harvesting for grafting.[1][2][3] In looksmaxxing communities it is mentioned mainly as a body-contouring option within the broader category of liposuction.

Published evidence consists mostly of surgeons' case series and small comparative studies; few randomized trials compare PAL with conventional suction-assisted liposuction, and the procedure is a surgical operation with the same general risk categories as other forms of liposuction.[1][4]
infobox: Local, regional or general, depending on extent

paras: In conventional liposuction a surgeon manually pushes and pulls a hollow cannula connected to suction through the fat layer. In power-assisted liposuction the cannula is attached to a handpiece that moves it back and forth at high frequency, a design that its advocates say reduces surgeon fatigue and speeds fat removal.[1] The procedure is usually combined with tumescent infiltration of local anesthetic solution.[1]

Reports describe PAL used with a pull-through approach to treat gynecomastia in men, in which fat and glandular tissue are removed through small incisions.[3] Surgeons have also used powered or vibrating cannulas to harvest fat for transfer, including large-volume gluteal fat grafting.[4][5]

Superficial liposuction, which works in the fat layer close to the skin to improve contour, has its own published complication analysis covering 2,398 cases, although that review concerns superficial technique in general rather than power assistance specifically.[6]

Complications described for liposuction in general include pain, bruising, swelling, contour irregularities, altered sensation, infection, bleeding, blood clots and, rarely, death, according to summaries of the literature.[1] A US survey of liposuction practice published in 2011 documented trends in how the procedure is performed and by whom.[7] Risk is reported to rise with the volume removed.[1]

A prospective randomized trial published in 2007 compared postoperative pain after power water-assisted and traditional liposuction.[8] A 2014 laboratory study compared adipose-derived stem cells obtained by power-assisted and manual aspiration in terms of viability and ability to differentiate into fat cells.[9] A registered 2026 trial (NCT07820397) is comparing adipose tissue viability after different liposuction approaches within the same patients.[10] A registered study of harmonic vibration liposuction (NCT07889427) enrolled 13 participants.[11] Most other published work is descriptive surgical technique reports.[3][4]

lore.intro: Power-assisted liposuction appears in forum discussions of body-contouring surgery, usually as one named option among liposuction technologies rather than as a looksmaxxing topic in its own right.

claims.claim: A vibrating cannula gives smoother, more precise fat removal than manual liposuction
claims.believers: Proponents, including some surgeons who use the technique, say the motion lets the cannula glide through fat with less force, which they associate with less surgeon fatigue and finer sculpting.[1]
claims.experts: Published comparisons are few; a randomized trial of postoperative pain used a power water-assisted device rather than a plain vibrating cannula, and surgical reports are largely descriptive.[8]

card.summary: A motorized, vibrating-cannula version of liposuction; documented in surgical reports but with little head-to-head trial evidence.
card.note: Surgical procedure; carries general liposuction risks.

quick.overview:
Power-assisted liposuction uses a cannula driven by a motor so it vibrates while moving through fat. It is a variant of ordinary liposuction used for body contouring, male chest reduction and fat harvesting.

Published work is mostly surgeons describing their technique. Few randomized comparisons with conventional liposuction exist.
quick.mechanism: A motorized handpiece moves the suction cannula rapidly back and forth, which proponents say reduces manual effort for the surgeon and eases passage through fat. It is typically paired with tumescent anesthetic solution.
quick.risks: As an operation, it shares liposuction risks reported in the literature, including pain, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, bleeding and clots, with rare deaths; risk is reported to increase with volume removed.
